screens.title: Incident Response & Disaster Recovery Planning
screens.narratorSegment: In production systems, outages and data loss are not a question of if, but when. This lesson helps you build structured incident response and disaster recovery plans specifically for PostgreSQL 12. You will learn how to detect and triage common incidents, which mitigation actions restore service quickly, and how to design an overall disaster recovery strategy that balances Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective. We use concrete PostgreSQL tools like physical backups, WAL archiving, streaming replication, and runbooks to turn policy into repeatable operations. I will show realistic examples: restarting a crashed service, promoting a hot standby, and performing a point-in-time restore from base backups plus archived WAL. We will also cover the softer but vital parts: communications, escalation, and blameless post-mortems so your team learns from incidents. By the end, you will be ready to create runbooks, choose backup and replication primitives to meet RTO/RPO targets, and run safe recovery drills on staging systems. Think of this chapter as the operational playbook that keeps your data available and your team calm under pressure.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Overview
Incident Response & Disaster Recovery
Operational playbook for PostgreSQL outages, replication failures, and recovery drills.
This chapter focuses on three pillars: a reproducible incident response plan, a disaster recovery strategy driven by RTO and RPO, and a culture of testing and post-mortems. Expect practical runbooks and PostgreSQL commands you can test in staging.

Coming up

Backups

screens.title: Skills Breakdown
screens.narratorSegment: Let's translate objectives into concrete skills you can validate. You will be able to write an incident runbook that includes symptoms, diagnostic commands, mitigation steps, escalation points, and expected outcomes. For example, a 'service down' runbook should list how to check the service, read logs, confirm disk space, attempt a safe restart, and escalate to failover if necessary. You'll also be able to choose and justify backup types: physical base backups for full restores and PITR, WAL archiving for continuous recovery, and logical dumps for schema-level restores. You will practice promoting a standby and restoring a base backup followed by WAL replay in a staging environment. Finally, you'll learn to perform post-mortems that produce action items: technical fixes, updated runbooks, or training tasks. These skills lead to measurable improvements: fewer repeated outages, faster recovery, and clearly assigned remediation tasks after incidents.

screens.title: Incident Response Plan for PostgreSQL
screens.narratorSegment: An incident response plan is a defined sequence of steps that converts alerts and user reports into coordinated actions. For PostgreSQL, incidents often include a down server, severe performance degradation, replication lag, disk full conditions, authentication failures, or data corruption. A strong plan names who does what and offers clear, runnable checks: how to verify the service is down, which logs to read, and what diagnostics to run. For example, a verified step for a down service is: confirm local psql connectivity, check systemd service status, then tail the PostgreSQL log for FATAL messages. That same plan should list quick mitigations: restart the service if safe, kill a runaway query, or fail over to a standby. A common misconception is that the plan must include a costly full restore as the first step. In practice, short mitigations often restore service faster and preserve data while a full restore runs in parallel. Concrete runbook fragments and diagnostic commands live in your plan so even junior staff can execute them under guidance. The core outcome is repeatability under pressure: the plan turns uncertainty into tasks and produces artifacts—logs, timelines, and decisions—that feed the post-mortem.

content.html:
Module 8 › Incident Response Plan
Definition & Purpose
A documented sequence that turns alerts into safe, repeatable recovery actions for PostgreSQL incidents.
Why it matters
  • Reduces time spent deciding what to do under pressure.
  • Enables consistent diagnostics and evidence collection for post-mortems.
  • Makes recovery actions executable by on-call staff.
Common mistake
Rushing to restore from backup before attempting quick mitigations or failover can needlessly increase downtime.
Key Takeaway

Write clear, small-step runbooks for each incident type so responders can act quickly and collect evidence for learning.

Runbook Example: 'PostgreSQL service down'
Symptoms, commands, mitigation, escalation, expected outputs.
Symptoms
Monitoring alert: service not responding; clients failing to connect.
Diagnostics
sudo systemctl status postgresql@12-main
sudo tail -n 200 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-12-main.log
psql -U postgres -c "SELECT 1;"
Mitigation
If logs show transient failure, attempt a restart; otherwise escalate. If replication exists and primary is irrecoverable, promote standby.
Escalation
Notify on-call DBA and application owners; include logs and timeline.
Example
A restart returned the service in 45 seconds; root cause later traced to an expired disk partition filling logs.
Pro tip
Keep short, copy-pasteable commands in the runbook and validate they work on a staging cluster matching production.

screens.title: Incident Lifecycle: Detect to Post-Mortem
screens.narratorSegment: Handle incidents as a lifecycle with seven explicit stages: detection, triage/assessment, diagnosis, mitigation, resolution, recovery, and post-mortem. Detection means monitoring alerts or user reports. A common detection source is monitoring rules that fire on failed connections, high latency, or replication lag. Triage asks: what is the impact and severity? Decide whether to page on-call staff, notify owners, or make a low-priority ticket. Diagnosis is where technical skill matters—use PostgreSQL logs, pg_stat_activity, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and OS tools to narrow the cause. Mitigation includes short-term actions that limit damage: restart the service, kill runaway queries, or fail over to a standby. Resolution is the permanent fix: configuration change, patch, or data restore. Recovery verifies full service and data integrity before returning to normal operations. Finally, the post-mortem documents timeline, root cause, impact, successes, and action items. A misconception is skipping post-mortem because the system is back; without it you miss preventive improvements. Concrete examples include running specific diagnostic commands and assigning action owners with deadlines so fixes actually happen. Incident Lifecycle: Detect to Post-Mortem means treat incidents as a life cycle; every incident should finish with a post-mortem and assigned action items.. In practical terms, a structured seven-step process for handling postgresql incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Incident Lifecycle
Seven steps
A consistent process reduces confusion and speeds recovery.
1
Detection
Monitoring alerts, health checks, or user reports.
2
Triage/Assessment
Assess severity, impacted services, and whether to page on-call.
3
Diagnosis
Use logs, pg_stat_activity, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and system tools to find root cause.
4
Mitigation
Short-term actions: restart, kill query, or failover to standby.
5
Resolution
Implement permanent fixes: config changes, patches, or restores.
6
Recovery
Verify data integrity and application connectivity before closing the incident.
7
Post-mortem
Create a blameless report with timeline, root cause, impact, and action items.
Diagnostic toolbox
Commands and views you will rely on during diagnosis.
# Check service
sudo systemctl status postgresql@12-main
# Tail logs
sudo tail -n 200 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-12-main.log
# Activity
psql -U postgres -c "SELECT pid, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle';"
# Replication
psql -U postgres -c "SELECT pid, state, sent_lsn, write_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;"
Example misconception
Assuming replication lag always indicates network problems. Often the primary is overloaded or a long-running transaction prevents WAL shipping.
Key Takeaway

Follow a lifecycle: detect, triage, diagnose, mitigate, recover, and learn. Every incident must end with a post-mortem and assigned actions.

screens.title: RTO and RPO: Metrics That Drive Design
screens.narratorSegment: Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective are the two metrics that guide your disaster recovery design. RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime after a disaster; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured backward from the recovery point. Translate business needs into these numbers: for example, an e-commerce checkout system may require an RTO of one hour and an RPO of 15 minutes, while an internal analytics database may tolerate longer windows. These metrics directly influence technical choices. A low RTO typically demands hot standbys with streaming replication so a standby can be promoted quickly. A low RPO leans on continuous WAL archiving or synchronous replication so little or no data is lost. A common misconception is treating backups alone as sufficient for low RPO: base backups without timely WAL archives can leave a large recovery gap. Practical example: to achieve RTO=1 hour and RPO=15 minutes, you would use physical streaming replication for fast promotion and continuous WAL archiving to fill any gap for PITR. Always verify by timed restore tests in staging: measure how long a restore actually takes and how much data is lost to confirm your stated RTO/RPO.

keyIdea.title: RTO/RPO principle
keyIdea.text: RTO defines how fast you must recover; RPO defines how much data loss is tolerable. Design backups and replication to meet those targets and verify with timed tests.

content.html:
Module 8 › RTO & RPO
Definitions
RTO — acceptable downtime. RPO — acceptable data loss window.
RTO (Recovery Time Objective)
How long you can be offline before business impact is unacceptable. Drives how quickly you must promote a standby or restore.
RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
How much data loss is tolerable, measured in time. Drives how often WAL is archived or whether synchronous replication is needed.
Misconception
Assuming a single backup plan meets both RTO and RPO. In reality, short RTO needs standbys; short RPO needs continuous WAL or synchronous replication.
Mapping metrics to technology
Choose technologies based on the RTO/RPO you set with stakeholders.
Low RTO
Use physical streaming replication with a hot standby to keep promotion time small.
Low RPO
Enable continuous WAL archiving and consider synchronous replication if zero or near-zero data loss is required.
PITR & Backups
Base backups plus WAL archives provide point-in-time recovery to any earlier moment within your retained WAL history.
Practical check
Run a timed restore in staging: measure how long restore takes and how current the data is; compare results to declared RTO/RPO and adjust architecture or runbooks accordingly.

screens.title: Backups & WAL Archiving
screens.narratorSegment: Backups are the foundation of disaster recovery. Physical base backups capture the entire data directory and are essential for point-in-time recovery when combined with WAL archives. WAL archiving continuously saves completed WAL segments so you can replay changes after restoring a base backup. Logical backups—pg_dump and pg_dumpall—produce S Q L that recreates schema and data; they are useful for schema migration and selective restores but are not a substitute for physical backups for PITR. Always configure archive_mode and a reliable archive_command so WAL segments are sent to a safe storage location. Importantly, backups must be tested: a backup that cannot be restored is worthless. Schedule full restore tests in a staging environment, measure the time to restore, and verify data integrity and application connectivity. A common mistake is keeping backups only on the same storage as the primary; store base backups and WAL archives off-site or in a separate region. Concrete example commands include pg_basebackup for base backups and a restore flow that copies base backup, configures recovery. signal, and sets restore_command to pull WAL segments from archive storage. Finish each test with a verification step: run application smoke tests and check recent rows for consistency.

keyIdea.title: Backup principle
keyIdea.text: Combine base backups with continuous WAL archiving for PITR, test restores regularly, and store archives off-site to meet RPO goals.

content.html:
Module 8 › Backups & WAL
Backup types
Choose the right backup forms for recovery objectives.
Physical backup (pg_basebackup)
Captures the data directory; used as a base for PITR when combined with WAL archives.
WAL archiving
Archive completed WAL segments using archive_command so you can replay changes during recovery.
Logical backups (pg_dump, pg_dumpall)
Produce SQL for schema/data export; good for migrations and selective restores but not sufficient for PITR alone.
Backup testing
Regularly restore base backups and replay WAL in staging. Verify application connectivity and data integrity within your RTO target.
Restore flow (conceptual)
Steps to restore a base backup and replay WAL to a recovery point.
# Take a base backup (primary)
pg_basebackup -h localhost -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/backup/base_backup -U postgres -P -Xs -R

# Ensure WAL archiving is working and archived WALs are available
# To restore on a new server:
# 1. Copy base backup into data directory
# 2. Create recovery.signal and set restore_command to copy WAL from archive
#    restore_command = 'cp /path/to/wal_archive/%f %p'
# 3. Start PostgreSQL and monitor replay until target time
Keep archives off-site and automate restore verification. Never test DR on production; use staging that mirrors production closely.
Key Takeaway

Backups plus WAL archiving enable PITR. Test restores and store archives off-site to meet RPO and validate RTO targets.

screens.title: Replication Strategies: Physical vs Logical
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is the backbone of many disaster recovery strategies, but not all replication types serve the same purpose. Physical streaming replication copies the exact data files and WAL stream to a standby. It keeps a near-identical copy, giving you a very low RPO and typically the fastest failover. Logical replication sends row-level changes and allows selective replication of tables and different major versions. That makes logical replication useful for version upgrades, selective sharing, and migrations, but it can yield higher replication lag or complexity for certain workloads. A concrete example: if your business requires that a standby can take over within minutes and you accept minimal data exposure, physical streaming replication with a hot standby is the right fit. If instead you need to replicate a subset of tables to a reporting database or to a different major version, logical replication is the right tool. A common misconception is that logical replication is automatically “better” because it’s flexible — in fact, logical replication cannot replace the byte-for-byte fidelity provided by a physical base backup and WAL for PITR. Key takeaway: pick physical streaming when you need tight RPO/RTO and logical replication when you need flexibility across schemas or versions. Which trade-offs in your environment push you to one approach over the other?

keyIdea.title: Match replication to requirements
keyIdea.text: Physical replication = low RTO/RPO; logical replication = selective copying and version flexibility.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 8.8 › Replication Strategies
Physical (Streaming)
Byte-for-byte standby via WAL streaming
Use when you need very low RPO and fast promotion. Requires base backup, compatible versions, and WAL shipping.
Low RPO
Fast failover
Logical Replication
Row-level logical changes across databases
Best for selective table replication, heterogeneous versions, or replicating to analytics systems. Requires publications and subscriptions.
Flexible topology
Potentially higher lag
Decision checklist
  • RTO and RPO targets — how quickly and how much data loss is acceptable?
  • Cross-version requirements — do you need replication across major versions?
  • Operational complexity — automation, monitoring, and failover testing required?
Example
E-commerce site: use physical streaming for low RPO on the primary and logical replication to push subset tables to a reporting cluster for analytics.
Key Takeaway

Choose replication by matching its guarantees to your RTO/RPO and operational constraints.

Common Mistake
Assuming logical replication alone is sufficient for PITR or low-RPO failover. It is not a substitute for base backups plus WAL archiving when you need point-in-time recovery.

screens.title: Failover and Switchover Procedures
screens.narratorSegment: Failover and switchover are two distinct operations you must practice. A failover is an emergency promotion of a standby when the primary fails unexpectedly. A switchover is a planned role swap used during maintenance. Both must be documented and tested. Start by confirming the primary is unreachable and that the standby has no conflicting writes. For emergency failover, typical steps are: verify replication lag and WAL availability, ensure application connections can be redirected, promote the standby using the promotion mechanism your setup supports, and reconfigure remaining standbys to follow the new primary. For example, on Debian-based packages you can promote with the cluster tool or with a simple trigger file approach: creating a trigger will cause the standby to exit recovery and become primary. A frequent misconception is skipping verification of replication health before promotion. Promoting a stale standby can cause data loss if WAL segments are missing. Another trap is neglecting to reconfigure clients and monitoring after promotion — your application must point to the newly promoted host. Test promotions in staging, simulate both planned and unplanned promotions, and document rollback steps. Closing thought: when was the last time your team practiced a promotion, and what did you learn from it?

A frequent misconception is skipping verification of replication health before promotion. Promoting a stale standby can cause data loss if WAL segments are missing. Another trap is neglecting to reconfigure clients and monitoring after promotion — your application must point to the newly promoted host. Test promotions in staging, simulate both planned and unplanned promotions, and document rollback steps. Closing thought: when was the last time your team practiced a promotion, and what did you learn from it?

keyIdea.text: Always verify replication health before promoting a standby and rehearse both failover and switchover in staging.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 8.8 › Failover & Switchover
Failover steps (emergency)
  1. Confirm primary unreachable and check WAL availability.
  2. Check replication lag: ensure standby has required WAL.
  3. Promote standby (command or trigger file).
  4. Repoint applications and update monitoring/HA proxies.
  5. Reconfigure remaining standbys to follow the new primary.
Common promote commands (examples used in testing):
# Promote a Debian/Ubuntu cluster
pg_ctlcluster 12 main promote

# Or, if using a trigger file in older recovery.conf setups
# touch /var/lib/postgresql/12/main/trigger_file
Switchover (planned)
Coordinate a graceful step-down of the primary, wait for standbys to catch up, switch traffic, then demote and reconfigure the former primary as a standby.
Pitfall
Promoting without verifying WAL continuity risks losing transactions that never arrived at the standby.
Pro Tip
Automate promotion checks with your cluster manager but always include a human-approved failback checklist for major incidents.

screens.title: Designing Clear, Actionable Runbooks
screens.narratorSegment: Runbooks turn incident knowledge into repeatable steps. A good runbook is concise, unambiguous, and ordered so a responder can follow it under pressure. It begins with the incident title, severity, triggers, and RTO/RPO targets. Then it lists verification commands, expected outputs, mitigation actions, and escalation contacts. For example, the 'PostgreSQL Service Down' runbook begins by verifying service status, checking logs for FATAL errors, and inspecting disk space. The runbook then suggests an attempted restart, verifies connectivity, and outlines next steps for disk-full or corruption scenarios. A practical tip is to include exact command lines and example outputs so responders recognize success or failure states. Another best practice is to mark safe rollback steps and to include an explicit safety note: never run destructive recovery on production without a tested plan. A common misconception is that runbooks must be long and exhaustive. In reality, clear short steps with pointers to deeper documentation make runbooks more usable during stress. Finally, schedule periodic drills where team members run the book on a staging system. After each drill, update the runbook with lessons learned. How could your runbooks be simplified so a new team member can follow them in an emergency?

Module 7 › Chapter 8.8 › Runbook Design
Runbook Template (concise)
Incident title · Severity · Triggers · RTO/RPO
# Verify
psql -U postgres -c "SELECT 1;"
sudo systemctl status postgresql@12-main

# Check logs
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-12-main.log

# Mitigation
sudo systemctl start postgresql@12-main
psql -U postgres -c "SELECT 1;"

# If disk full: identify and clear old logs
sudo df -h /var/lib/postgresql/12/main

# Escalation
Alert: oncall-db@example.com
Checklist for a good runbook
  • Short steps with exact commands
  • Expected outputs or success indicators
  • Clear escalation and ownership
  • Safety and rollback notes
Try this
Create a short runbook for a simple incident and practice it in a staging environment. Note any ambiguous steps and refine them immediately.
Safety Note
Never execute destructive recovery steps on production. Use a staging mirror for validation and drills.

screens.title: Conducting Blameless Post-Mortems
screens.narratorSegment: A post-mortem is a structured, blameless review of an incident that focuses on cause, impact, and prevention. Its goal is to learn, not to place blame. Start by assembling a timeline of events: when the alert fired, who took actions, what commands were run, and what changed. Next perform root cause analysis to identify the underlying failure mode — whether configuration, capacity, software bug, or human error. Assess the impact: which users or data were affected, and how long? Then document what went well and what could be improved. Action items are the most important outcome: they must be specific, measurable, and assigned to an owner with a deadline. Examples of action items include: update a runbook to clarify a restart step, add a monitoring alert for disk usage at 80 percent, or automate failover verification. A common misconception is that a post-mortem is optional for small incidents. In fact, even small incidents reveal process or visibility gaps and help prevent larger failures. Finally, close the loop by tracking action-item completion and revisiting the post-mortem after fixes are applied. Ask yourself: which single change would most reduce the chance of this incident repeating?

keyIdea.text: Post-mortems create measurable improvements through timelines, root-cause analysis, and tracked action items.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 8.8 › Post-Mortem Analysis
Post-mortem structure
  1. Timeline — chronological events and timestamps.
  2. Root cause analysis — why the failure occurred.
  3. Impact assessment — users, data, business effect.
  4. What went well — effective responses or tools.
  5. Action items — specific owners and deadlines.
Example action items
  • Add WAL archiving health check and alert — owner: ops — due in 7 days.
  • Update 'service down' runbook with log paths — owner: oncall — due in 3 days.
  • Schedule quarterly failover drills — owner: team lead — due in 30 days.
Blameless culture
Encourage open reporting and focus on systems, not individuals. This increases transparency and learning.
Key Takeaway
A short, tracked list of action items is more valuable than a long narrative. Measure closure and verify fixes.
Mistake to avoid
Leaving action items vague or unassigned. That leads to repeated incidents and wasted time.

screens.title: DR Testing Workflow: Base Backups, WAL, and Promotion
screens.narratorSegment: Testing your disaster recovery workflow is the most important investment you can make. The workflow usually starts with a base backup and WAL archiving. In tests, you take a base backup, ensure WAL segments archive successfully, simulate a primary failure, promote a standby, or perform a full restore to a clean server and replay WAL to a recovery point. I will not read commands aloud; instead, notice that the code block below is a safe, stepwise script you can run in a staging environment. After running each command, verify expected messages in logs, check that WAL files were archived, and confirm the application can connect after recovery. A common misconception is assuming a backup exists is the same as a recoverable backup. Always restore to a separate instance, verify data integrity, and validate connectivity. In practice, run this workflow quarterly or after major changes and document elapsed time versus your RTO target. After a successful test, update your playbooks with measured restore times and any adjustments needed. When did you last restore a backup to a new server and confirm application behavior?

keyIdea.text: Always perform restore tests and measure elapsed time to validate RTO and RPO commitments.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 8.8 › DR Test Commands
Representative DR test commands (staging only)
# 1. Take a physical base backup on primary
pg_basebackup -h localhost -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/backup/base_backup -U postgres -P -Xs -R

# 2. Ensure WAL archiving is functioning (check logs for "archived WAL file")
# 3. Simulate primary failure
sudo systemctl stop postgresql@12-main

# 4. Promote standby (example)
pg_ctlcluster 12 main promote
# Or create trigger file if configured
# touch /var/lib/postgresql/12/main/trigger_file

# 5. Restore from base backup to a new server and replay WAL
# a) Initialize new data directory and copy base backup
# b) Create recovery.signal and set restore_command
#    restore_command = 'cp /path/to/wal_archive/%f %p'
#    recovery_target_time = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
# c) Start PostgreSQL
pg_ctlcluster 12 main start

# 6. Verify data integrity and application connectivity after recovery
Validation checklist
  • Confirm WAL files archived and replayed without errors.
  • Run basic application health checks and sample queries.
  • Check for missing objects or corruption reports in logs.
  • Record elapsed time and compare to RTO target.
Key Takeaway
Measure restore times and validate data integrity regularly. That is the only reliable way to trust your DR plan.
Safety Reminder
Run these commands only in staging or tightly controlled environments that mirror production; never perform destructive tests on a live primary.

fullNarratorScript:
In production systems, outages and data loss are not a question of if, but when. This lesson helps you build structured incident response and disaster recovery plans specifically for PostgreSQL 12. You will learn how to detect and triage common incidents, which mitigation actions restore service quickly, and how to design an overall disaster recovery strategy that balances Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective. We use concrete PostgreSQL tools like physical backups, WAL archiving, streaming replication, and runbooks to turn policy into repeatable operations. I will show realistic examples: restarting a crashed service, promoting a hot standby, and performing a point-in-time restore from base backups plus archived WAL. We will also cover the softer but vital parts: communications, escalation, and blameless post-mortems so your team learns from incidents. By the end, you will be ready to create runbooks, choose backup and replication primitives to meet RTO/RPO targets, and run safe recovery drills on staging systems. Think of this chapter as the operational playbook that keeps your data available and your team calm under pressure.

These objectives set clear operational skills you will gain. First, you will develop a structured incident response plan that details detection, triage, diagnosis, mitigation, resolution, recovery, and post-mortem steps for PostgreSQL incidents. A concrete outcome is a written runbook for at least one common outage scenario that a team member can follow. Second, you will define Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective for a database, understand their practical meaning, and map technologies like streaming replication and WAL archiving to meet those targets. Third, you will design a backup and replication strategy: choosing base backups, WAL archiving, and streaming replication to satisfy RTO/RPO, including where to store backups off-site and how frequently to test restores. Fourth, you will create and test runbooks and post-mortem templates so incidents lead to measurable improvements. Each objective pairs a technical skill with a practice habit: document, test, and update. Together these skills reduce downtime, limit data loss, and make responses repeatable and blameless.

Let's translate objectives into concrete skills you can validate. You will be able to write an incident runbook that includes symptoms, diagnostic commands, mitigation steps, escalation points, and expected outcomes. For example, a 'service down' runbook should list how to check the service, read logs, confirm disk space, attempt a safe restart, and escalate to failover if necessary. You'll also be able to choose and justify backup types: physical base backups for full restores and PITR, WAL archiving for continuous recovery, and logical dumps for schema-level restores. You will practice promoting a standby and restoring a base backup followed by WAL replay in a staging environment. Finally, you'll learn to perform post-mortems that produce action items: technical fixes, updated runbooks, or training tasks. These skills lead to measurable improvements: fewer repeated outages, faster recovery, and clearly assigned remediation tasks after incidents.

An incident response plan is a defined sequence of steps that converts alerts and user reports into coordinated actions. For PostgreSQL, incidents often include a down server, severe performance degradation, replication lag, disk full conditions, authentication failures, or data corruption. A strong plan names who does what and offers clear, runnable checks: how to verify the service is down, which logs to read, and what diagnostics to run. For example, a verified step for a down service is: confirm local psql connectivity, check systemd service status, then tail the PostgreSQL log for FATAL messages. That same plan should list quick mitigations: restart the service if safe, kill a runaway query, or fail over to a standby. A common misconception is that the plan must include a costly full restore as the first step. In practice, short mitigations often restore service faster and preserve data while a full restore runs in parallel. Concrete runbook fragments and diagnostic commands live in your plan so even junior staff can execute them under guidance. The core outcome is repeatability under pressure: the plan turns uncertainty into tasks and produces artifacts—logs, timelines, and decisions—that feed the post-mortem.

Handle incidents as a lifecycle with seven explicit stages: detection, triage/assessment, diagnosis, mitigation, resolution, recovery, and post-mortem. Detection means monitoring alerts or user reports. A common detection source is monitoring rules that fire on failed connections, high latency, or replication lag. Triage asks: what is the impact and severity? Decide whether to page on-call staff, notify owners, or make a low-priority ticket. Diagnosis is where technical skill matters—use PostgreSQL logs, pg_stat_activity, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and OS tools to narrow the cause. Mitigation includes short-term actions that limit damage: restart the service, kill runaway queries, or fail over to a standby. Resolution is the permanent fix: configuration change, patch, or data restore. Recovery verifies full service and data integrity before returning to normal operations. Finally, the post-mortem documents timeline, root cause, impact, successes, and action items. A misconception is skipping post-mortem because the system is back; without it you miss preventive improvements. Concrete examples include running specific diagnostic commands and assigning action owners with deadlines so fixes actually happen. Incident Lifecycle: Detect to Post-Mortem means treat incidents as a life cycle; every incident should finish with a post-mortem and assigned action items.. In practical terms, a structured seven-step process for handling postgresql incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective are the two metrics that guide your disaster recovery design. RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime after a disaster; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured backward from the recovery point. Translate business needs into these numbers: for example, an e-commerce checkout system may require an RTO of one hour and an RPO of 15 minutes, while an internal analytics database may tolerate longer windows. These metrics directly influence technical choices. A low RTO typically demands hot standbys with streaming replication so a standby can be promoted quickly. A low RPO leans on continuous WAL archiving or synchronous replication so little or no data is lost. A common misconception is treating backups alone as sufficient for low RPO: base backups without timely WAL archives can leave a large recovery gap. Practical example: to achieve RTO=1 hour and RPO=15 minutes, you would use physical streaming replication for fast promotion and continuous WAL archiving to fill any gap for PITR. Always verify by timed restore tests in staging: measure how long a restore actually takes and how much data is lost to confirm your stated RTO/RPO.

Backups are the foundation of disaster recovery. Physical base backups capture the entire data directory and are essential for point-in-time recovery when combined with WAL archives. WAL archiving continuously saves completed WAL segments so you can replay changes after restoring a base backup. Logical backups—pg_dump and pg_dumpall—produce S Q L that recreates schema and data; they are useful for schema migration and selective restores but are not a substitute for physical backups for PITR. Always configure archive_mode and a reliable archive_command so WAL segments are sent to a safe storage location. Importantly, backups must be tested: a backup that cannot be restored is worthless. Schedule full restore tests in a staging environment, measure the time to restore, and verify data integrity and application connectivity. A common mistake is keeping backups only on the same storage as the primary; store base backups and WAL archives off-site or in a separate region. Concrete example commands include pg_basebackup for base backups and a restore flow that copies base backup, configures recovery. signal, and sets restore_command to pull WAL segments from archive storage. Finish each test with a verification step: run application smoke tests and check recent rows for consistency.

Replication is the backbone of many disaster recovery strategies, but not all replication types serve the same purpose. Physical streaming replication copies the exact data files and WAL stream to a standby. It keeps a near-identical copy, giving you a very low RPO and typically the fastest failover. Logical replication sends row-level changes and allows selective replication of tables and different major versions. That makes logical replication useful for version upgrades, selective sharing, and migrations, but it can yield higher replication lag or complexity for certain workloads. A concrete example: if your business requires that a standby can take over within minutes and you accept minimal data exposure, physical streaming replication with a hot standby is the right fit. If instead you need to replicate a subset of tables to a reporting database or to a different major version, logical replication is the right tool. A common misconception is that logical replication is automatically “better” because it’s flexible — in fact, logical replication cannot replace the byte-for-byte fidelity provided by a physical base backup and WAL for PITR. Key takeaway: pick physical streaming when you need tight RPO/RTO and logical replication when you need flexibility across schemas or versions. Which trade-offs in your environment push you to one approach over the other?

Test promotions in staging, simulate both planned and unplanned promotions, and document rollback steps.
